subskill: Linear function in context: net change from rates given per day and per week
prompt: A food bank has 4,200 cans in stock. Starting now, it receives donated cans at a constant rate of 340 cans per day, and it gives out cans at a constant rate of 1,890 cans per week. If both rates continue, how many cans will the food bank have in stock 3 weeks and 4 days from now?
explanation:
Giving out 1,890 cans per week at a constant rate is 1,890/7 = 270 cans per day, so the stock grows by 340 − 270 = 70 cans per day. Three weeks and 4 days is 3(7) + 4 = 25 days, so the stock will be 4,200 + 70(25) = 5,950 cans.

6160 comes from rounding 3 weeks and 4 days up to 4 full weeks (28 days). 6580 comes from treating 3 weeks and 4 days as 34 days. 7030 comes from subtracting the weekly 1,890 only for the 3 full weeks and counting only donations during the last 4 days, even though cans are given out at a constant rate every day.

subskill: Linear model with literal constants: constant is value at t = 0, not at a stated start
prompt: Biologists model the number of sea turtle nests on a beach with the function N(t) = a + bt, where a and b are constants and t is the number of years after 2018. Monitoring of the beach began in 2021, when 340 nests were counted, and in 2027, 610 nests were counted. Both counts fit the model exactly. What is the value of a + b?
explanation:
In the model, 2021 is t = 3 and 2027 is t = 9. So a + 3b = 340 and a + 9b = 610. Subtracting gives 6b = 270, so b = 45, and then a = 340 − 3(45) = 205. Therefore a + b = 205 + 45 = 250.

295 comes from counting 2021 as t = 2 and 2027 as t = 8, which gives b = 45 and a = 250. 280 comes from dividing the increase of 270 by 9, the number of years from 2018 to 2027, instead of by the 6 years from 2021 to 2027, which gives b = 30 and a = 250. 160 comes from finding a = 205 and b = 45 correctly and then computing a − b instead of a + b.
solve: const b=(610-340)/(9-3); const a=340-3*b; return a+b;

distractor_solve.160: const b=(610-340)/(9-3); const a=340-3*b; return a-b;
distractor_solve.280: const b=(610-340)/9; const a=340-3*b; return a+b;
distractor_solve.295: const b=(610-340)/(8-2); const a=340-2*b; return a+b;

subskill: Linear inequalities in context: pricing tier and a second binding constraint
prompt: A print shop charges a $12 setup fee on every order. In addition, an order of fewer than 400 pages costs $0.085 per page, and an order of 400 pages or more costs $0.06 per page for every page in the order. The shop's printer needs 3 minutes to warm up and then prints 26 pages per minute, and every order must be finished within 20 minutes of turning the printer on. A customer can spend at most $40 on one order. What is the greatest number of pages the customer can order?
explanation:
Time: after the 3-minute warm-up, 17 minutes remain, so the printer can print at most 17(26) = 442 pages. Cost: after the $12 fee, $28 remains for pages. At the under-400 rate, 0.085p ≤ 28 gives at most 329 pages. At the 400-or-more rate, 0.06p ≤ 28 gives p ≤ 466.6..., so at most 466 pages, and the lower rate applies to any order of 400 or more pages. Both conditions must hold, so the greatest order is 442 pages, which is at least 400 pages and costs 12 + 0.06(442) = $38.52.

466 comes from using only the cost condition and ignoring the printing time. 329 comes from using only the under-400 rate and never checking whether a larger order qualifies for the lower rate. 266 comes from subtracting the $12 fee twice, (40 − 24)/0.06.
solve: const t=(20-3)*26; const c=Math.floor((40-12)/0.06+1e-9); let p=Math.min(t,c); if(p<400) p=Math.min(t,Math.floor((40-12)/0.085+1e-9)); return p;

subskill: System in context: asked quantity is a combination of the two rates
prompt: A workshop has two machines, A and B, each producing parts at its own constant rate. On Monday, machine A ran alone for 2 hours, and then machines A and B ran together for 3 more hours; 1,010 parts were produced in all. On Tuesday, machine B ran alone for 1 hour, and then machines A and B ran together for 4 more hours; 1,185 parts were produced in all. How many parts would the two machines produce running together for 6 hours?
explanation:
Let a and b be the machines' rates in parts per hour. On Monday machine A ran 5 hours and machine B ran 3 hours, so 5a + 3b = 1,010. On Tuesday machine A ran 4 hours and machine B ran 5 hours, so 4a + 5b = 1,185. Adding Monday's equation to twice Tuesday's gives 13a + 13b = 1,010 + 2,370 = 3,380, so a + b = 260 parts per hour. (Solving the system directly gives a = 115 and b = 145, with the same sum.) Running together for 6 hours, the machines produce 6(260) = 1,560 parts.

1515 comes from assuming the two machines have the same rate and using only Monday's total: 1,010 parts in 8 machine-hours, times 12 machine-hours. 1580 comes from the same equal-rate assumption applied only to Tuesday's total: 1,185 parts in 9 machine-hours, times 12 machine-hours. 1740 comes from finding b = 145 and then multiplying by 12, as if both machines produced at machine B's rate.
